result_and_mechanism_map.title: Maass spectral data packages central Hecke values into a positive weighted family
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The paper fixes Laplacian eigenvalues, simultaneous Hecke eigenforms, parity, and their Hecke series, creating the spectral coordinates later visible as poles and exponential sums. This setup explains why central Hecke values, rather than arbitrary coefficients, control fourth-moment phenomena.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Poles of Z₂ encode the hyperbolic spectrum and central Hecke values
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The modified Mellin transform of the fourth zeta moment has a meromorphic continuation whose off-real poles occur at spectral parameters, with residues weighted by cubes of central Hecke values; additional poles track zeta zeros. This makes Z₂ a bridge between moment errors and spectral cancellation.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Modified Mellin inversion avoids the origin while retaining ordinary Mellin structure
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: A reflection-and-truncation device identifies the modified transform over [1,∞) with an ordinary Mellin transform, transferring Fourier/Mellin inversion to recover the original function under explicit integrability and continuity conditions.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Products in the original variable become transform convolution and Parseval identities
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Two lemmas transfer the ordinary Mellin product formula and Parseval identity to the modified transform, supplying both a convolution law and an exact weighted L² identity. These become the algebraic engine for later moment and recurrence arguments.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Localization and contour shifting transfer transform mean squares back to the source function
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: A localized Parseval inequality bounds the mean square of a truncated modified transform by a weighted source norm. A converse-style lemma then smooths a dyadic source interval, shifts past the transform’s polar part, truncates by repeated integration by parts, and uses Cauchy–Schwarz plus Parseval to control the source mean square by the transform mean square.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Fourth-moment error bounds set the attainable scale for Z₂ mean squares
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The section defines E₂(T), inventories its mean-square, pointwise, omega, and integral behavior, and records how an assumed pointwise exponent for E₂ feeds an existing Z₂ mean-square estimate. This establishes the unconditional baseline and identifies which scales are already essentially optimal.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Removing the polar part makes E₂ and Z₂ mean squares Parseval dual
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Integration by parts decomposes Z₂ into an explicit pole at one plus the transform of E₂. After subtracting the polar part, Parseval gives an exact weighted identity; contour propagation then shows that a boundary Z₂ mean-square bound recovers the best known E₂ and twelfth-moment estimates.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: A source-to-transform transfer forces a lower bound for every interior Z₂ mean square
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Theorem 1 applies the mean-square transfer lemma to Hardy’s real Z-function: a known lower bound for the eighth zeta moment cannot be supported unless the Z₂ transform has at least the stated mean-square size. This supplies evidence that the later conjectured exponent is sharp from below.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: A smoothed Mellin decomposition propagates Z₂ control between vertical lines
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Theorem 2 partitions the transform into low, middle, and tail ranges, handles the tail via E₂ and localized Parseval, reinserts Z₂ by Mellin inversion on the middle range, and truncates the resulting convolution by repeated integration by parts. The result is a convexity-type mean-square and pointwise transfer from a line c to a line σ.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Bootstrapping the propagation theorem sharpens mean-square bounds near σ=1
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Feeding a previously known estimate on one vertical line into Theorem 2 yields an improved exponent for σ at least 5/6, demonstrating how the transfer inequality can bootstrap existing information.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Conjecture 1 posits the lower-bound scale and would optimize E₂ and the eighth moment
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The proposed Z₂ mean-square bound matches Theorem 1’s scale up to ε. A smoothed inverse-transform argument would then give square-root-size E₂, while the earlier transfer inequality would give the conjecturally optimal eighth moment.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: The eighth-moment conjecture is equivalent to a weaker piecewise Z₂ mean-square bound
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The paper cannot prove equivalence with Conjecture 1 itself, but shows that the optimal eighth moment yields a piecewise transform estimate and that the near-one portion of that estimate recovers the eighth moment. This precisely locates the gap between a desired conjecture and a provably equivalent surrogate.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Conjecture 2 is a Lindelöf-type pointwise claim equivalent to vertical decay
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: A pointwise subpower conjecture for Z₂ is reformulated as the stronger-looking decay t^{1/2−σ+ε}. The proof shows self-improvement: smooth truncation, contour shift to near the critical line, and a second integral representation convert the original uniform bound into decay across the strip.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: RH, Lindelöf, E₂, and eighth-moment implications are not interchangeable
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The author explicitly warns that the optimal E₂ bound and eighth-moment bound do not appear to imply one another, and that RH does not apparently yield the former even though Lindelöf yields the latter. This prevents collapsing distinct conjectural channels.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Central Hecke values require cancellation beyond positive short-interval bounds
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The section compares Lindelöf-type cancellation in ordinary Dirichlet sums with central Hecke-value sums. Known positivity gives strong average and pointwise bounds but cannot improve an unweighted unit spectral interval; inserting an oscillatory phase is therefore identified as the missing source of square-root cancellation.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Two zeta problems reduce to the same oscillatory spectral phase
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Both E₂ and the eighth moment are expressed through short spectral sums weighted by central Hecke values. Absolute-value use of the known bound is too weak; Stirling asymptotics of the residue factor exposes an oscillatory phase, revealing that both applications demand essentially the same cancellation problem.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Conjecture 3 posits square-root cancellation in unit spectral intervals
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The conjecture asks an oscillatory unit-interval sum of positive central Hecke weights to save a square root over the best unweighted bound. The paper traces this hypothesis separately to optimal E₂ and eighth-moment bounds, noting an additional spectral-error step needed for the latter.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Motohashi’s transformation formula offers a smoothed route but not the unsmoothed target
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The author proposes embedding the unit-interval exponential sum in a spectral transformation formula with an even Gaussian-localized test function and adjustable window G. The key obstruction is explicit: progress for the Gaussian-smoothed transform would not automatically control the unsmoothed sum required by the zeta applications.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Any one of the three conjectures yields a strengthened zeta-weighted Dirichlet-polynomial mean value
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The paper identifies a shared downstream inequality for arbitrary Dirichlet coefficients and compares it with prior unconditional bounds, showing that the conjectures control more than the motivating E₂ and moment problems.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Spectral residues heuristically link Conjecture 3 to Conjecture 2 and motivate a new unconditional bound
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Shifting a contour across Z₂’s spectral poles predicts a short residue sum. Ignoring its oscillation and using only the known average gives t^{1−σ+ε}; using Conjecture 3 would give the pointwise conjecture. The article then isolates the former as a theorem away from poles.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Oscillation removes an artificial smoothing-width restriction in the pointwise bound
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The proof revisits a spectral decomposition based on a Gaussian-smoothed fourth moment. A previous saddle estimate required ξ≥1/3; expanding the saddle more accurately, isolating the phase derivative, and applying a first-derivative test controls the formerly troublesome contribution for every positive ξ, permitting ξ≈0 and yielding the claimed pointwise exponent.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Any pointwise improvement for Z₂ propagates quantitatively to E₂ and zeta moments
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The theorem’s boundary value recovers known mean-square and moment bounds; more generally, a hypothetical exponent ρ for Z₂ gives an explicit improved exponent for E₂. This quantifies why spectral exponential-sum progress is the bottleneck.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Analytic continuation of every Z_k is equivalent to the Lindelöf moment hierarchy
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Mellin inversion converts smoothed 2k-th zeta moments into contour integrals of Z_k. Regular polynomial-growth continuation just beyond σ=1 implies all Lindelöf-strength moments, while integration by parts gives the converse; taken over all k, this is equivalent to Lindelöf.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Z₁ satisfies the conjectured mean-square scale but not the pointwise analogue
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The k=1 transform already has the mean-square exponent conjectured for Z₂ and a dyadic refinement, yet its Lindelöf-type pointwise bound remains out of reach. This demonstrates that mean-square success does not automatically resolve pointwise control even in the simpler case.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Products of zeta moments induce a convolution recurrence among Z_k
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Double Mellin inversion expresses a 2(k+l)-th moment through Z_k and Z_l with frequency coupling, while the modified-transform convolution lemma gives a direct recurrence Z_{k+l} as a vertical convolution. This suggests building higher-moment information compositionally from lower transforms.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: The eighth moment heuristically forces Conjecture 3’s square-root scale
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Taking k=l=2 in the transform factorization and isolating the discrete spectral contribution turns the known eighth-moment lower scale into a lower bound for a supremum of the same short oscillatory Hecke sums. After truncation and Stirling analysis, this argues that Conjecture 3 would be essentially optimal.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: The short-interval second moment is a critical partition function
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The paper treats the integral of |ζ|² over a fixed short interval as a statistical-mechanical partition function. Although its global t-average is of order log T, the motivating question is its typical size, exposing a distinction between an average dominated by rare events and a typical local mass.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Fractional moments reveal a critical square-root logarithmic renormalization
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Theorem 1 uniformly bounds all fractional moments 0≤q≤1 by a scale containing a nontrivial denominator depending on (1−q)log log T. Optimizing Markov’s inequality in q turns this into a typical-size/tail bound smaller than the global mean by a square-root log-log factor.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: The exponent two marks the freezing transition and links partition mass to maxima
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Random-matrix ‘moments of moments’ motivate the distributional program, while the dominance scale of ζ moments explains why β=1 is the critical boundary between many and rare large values in a bounded interval. This identifies the partition function studied by Theorem 1 as the critical-chaos observable relevant to local maxima.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Theorem 2 matches the first two FHK terms but not the full maximum law
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The Fyodorov–Hiary–Keating conjecture predicts a centered distribution for the short-interval log maximum with a −3/4 log log log T correction. Theorem 2 proves an upper-tail estimate that yields this leading and second-order behavior for almost all t, while an extra third-order term and poly-log-log-log losses remain.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: A smooth/rough factorization isolates Euler-product structure without discarding large primes
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The proof approximates ζ by a Dirichlet polynomial, then in mean square by a product of a short P-smooth sum and a longer P-rough sum. Only the smooth factor is converted to an Euler product and compared with a Steinhaus model; the independent rough factor contributes its mean square. Multiscale good events and a recursive q argument import the critical-chaos saving.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Cauchy localization and a lower smooth-factor barrier convert maxima into a ballot problem
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: For Theorem 2, Cauchy’s formula replaces an unknown maximizing point by integrals around a 1/log T rectangle. A fourth-moment argument shows a large total product usually forces the smooth factor above a threshold; after derandomization this becomes a terminal lower barrier, and a Gaussian ballot estimate yields the characteristic 3/4 saving.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Keeping the rough factor preserves scale, while multi-band factorization may reduce the main loss
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Unlike earlier approaches that shorten prime sums or shift off the critical line, this method retains the large-prime contribution and pays for it only through mean-square control. The author proposes—without checked details—splitting into more prime bands so successive largeness transfers incur smaller losses.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Matching lower bounds fail at the step from integrated mass to a single extreme
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: A lower counterpart to Theorem 1 appears approachable by importing the random lower-moment proof under growth constraints. For Theorem 2, however, a large restricted integral may arise from several moderately large ζ values rather than one extreme, and the rough factor lacks the control needed to distinguish these cases.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Dirichlet-polynomial time averages approximate Steinhaus expectations
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: A mean-value lemma identifies the diagonal time average with the orthogonality relation of a Steinhaus random multiplicative function and controls off-diagonal error by Hilbert’s inequality. When polynomial length fits the averaging interval, this supplies the basic deterministic-to-random transfer.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Even moments of prime polynomials remain controlled when multiplied by a structured Dirichlet polynomial
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Lemma 2 bounds high even moments of a prime/prime-square polynomial, both alone and weighted by another Dirichlet polynomial. Its proof expands multiplicative coincidences, uses mean-value orthogonality, and controls multiplicities by a tailored divisor weight, enabling later union bounds and Taylor-remainder estimates.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: The approximate functional equation admits a shorter smooth/rough product approximation
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: After the symmetric approximate functional equation, Lemma 3 shows uniformly near the critical line that the principal Dirichlet polynomial is close in mean square to independent-range P-smooth and P-rough factors. The proof freezes the t-dependent endpoint locally, removes tail and oversized smooth parts, and bounds the small σ shift.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: A band-limited majorant turns barrier indicators into controlled polynomial expansions
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Convolving a Beurling–Selberg majorant with an interval indicator produces a smooth near-indicator with bounded range, small leakage outside an expanded interval, and explicit derivative bounds. Taylor truncations of this function can therefore be inserted into Dirichlet-polynomial averages.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Theorem 1 is reduced to a restricted average and a rare bad-event estimate
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The proof discretizes h at prime-dependent scales, factors the Euler product into logarithmic prime blocks, and defines a two-sided multiscale good event. Key Proposition 1 controls the partition mass on that event with the critical q-dependent saving; Key Proposition 2 makes its complement exponentially rare.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: A q-recursion absorbs the bad set and closes Theorem 1 uniformly
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: After approximation error is separated, near-q=1 cases follow from a second moment. For smaller q, splitting by the good event, raising the bad-event contribution to a slightly larger exponent q′, and using its exponential rarity gives a contraction R(δ)≤C+e^{-C/2}R(δ/2), iterated back to the base range.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Union bounds plus optimized high moments make multiscale barrier failure rare
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Key Proposition 2 expands logarithms of partial Euler products into prime and prime-square sums, unions over discrete h-scales, and applies Lemma 2 with an optimized moment order. Entropy from the number of discretization points is canceled by the logarithmic padding in the barrier.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Independence separates the rough variance from the critical smooth Euler-product estimate
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Lemma 4 factors the random restricted expectation because its good event depends only on primes up to P. The truncated smooth sum is completed to an Euler product in mean square, the rough factor contributes log T/log P, and a prior critical-chaos proposition supplies the q-dependent saving.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Smooth barrier products are Taylor-expanded, averaged, and reconstructed in the random model
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Key Proposition 1 majorizes the deterministic good event by a product of smooth functions, truncates each at controlled degree, bounds all Taylor remainders by high moments, and uses the mean-value lemma to replace the polynomialized time integral by a Steinhaus expectation. Reassembling the smooth functions exposes the imported random barrier event and completes the bound.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: A fourth moment forces large total mass to pass through a large smooth factor
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Lemma 5 bounds the fourth moment of the smooth×rough product on points where the smooth factor is below log P/V. Expanding the rough fourth power and applying the mean-value theorem yields a V^{-2} saving but a log T/log P loss, quantitatively exporting a ζ largeness condition to the smooth component.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: A three-block Gaussian decomposition yields two independent barrier savings
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Probability Result 1 bounds a Gaussian walk that stays below an upper barrier and ends in a narrow terminal window. Splitting the walk into early, middle, and reversed late blocks separates an upper-barrier probability, an interval-density factor, and a terminal-barrier probability, producing one square-root factor and one squared factor.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Theorem 2 is reduced to a U-dependent rare event and a doubly restricted random average
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: A finer h discretization and a one-sided logarithmic barrier define G̃_t. Key Proposition 3 bounds its failure by e^{-2U}; Key Proposition 4 controls the smooth×rough mean square when both the upper barrier and a smooth-factor lower threshold hold, with two ballot-type factors.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Cauchy’s rectangle turns an unknown maximum into three controllable integral regimes
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: At the maximizing h, the approximate functional equation and Cauchy’s formula replace a large value by one of four small-box contour integrals. Each vertical integral is split into factorization error, small-smooth contribution, and large-smooth/good-event contribution, controlled respectively by Lemma 3, Lemma 5, and Key Proposition 4; horizontal sides are handled by summing over a fixed grid.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: The modified good event retains an e^{-2U} failure rate despite finer discretization
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Key Proposition 3 repeats the optimized high-moment union bound with the new one-sided barrier, U padding, and denser h grid. The three log-log-log padding powers absorb grid entropy, and the P restriction keeps the optimized moment within the mean-value length limit.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: A truncated exponential approximates the smooth sum at scale-adapted h points
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Lemma 6 replaces the P-smooth Dirichlet polynomial by a truncated exponential of prime-power sums whose h argument is discretized at the prime’s natural scale. Mean-value orthogonality reduces the error to coefficient truncation plus phase mismatch; Taylor/Mertens estimates make both small.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Conditioning away tiny primes lets the Gaussian ballot theorem control the lower endpoint
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Lemma 7 augments the random good event with a strong lower bound on the full product. It conditions on the contribution of the smallest-prime blocks to restore the hypotheses of an imported Euler-product-to-Gaussian comparison, then applies Probability Result 1 to obtain separate upper-barrier and terminal-window factors.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: The lower smooth threshold is transferred to a random terminal barrier and closes Key Proposition 4
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: On G̃_t, the truncated exponential from Lemma 6 is comparable to the Euler-product block product, so a large smooth sum implies a terminal lower product barrier except for a controlled approximation error. The proof then repeats smooth-majorant Taylor derandomization with a shifted j=0 constraint, invokes Lemma 7, and checks degree, leakage, length, and truncation errors.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Parity-split program for representing integer zeta values by logarithmic moments
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The introduction explicitly organizes prior isolated log-sine and log-sinh evaluations into two general tasks: rederive odd zeta representations, add an even analogue, prove general log-sine formulas, and relate the circular and hyperbolic integral families. This supplies the source's conceptual comparison even though the displayed target formulas are damaged.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Exponential denominators rewritten as log-sinh kernels
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The visible identity factoring an exponential difference through a hyperbolic sine explains why substitutions in a standard zeta-integral kernel generate powers of log(2 sinh(theta/2)). The special choice of an algebraic endpoint then creates paired auxiliary integrals to be evaluated.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Auxiliary-integral evaluation by reciprocal substitutions, integration by parts, and parity recombination
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The prose documents a reusable evaluation pipeline: evaluate two auxiliary families, transform their integrals by substitutions, reduce a remaining logarithmic integral by integration by parts, derive separate even and odd relations, and substitute those relations back into the original pair. This is the mechanism leading to the Section 2 representation theorem.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: A complex contour identity converted into log-sine moment families
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The source defines B(theta)=log(2 sin(theta/2)), integrates along a specified unit-circle arc, applies a complex affine substitution, and splits the result into real-variable integrals. Taking real and imaginary parts at opposite parity choices, then invoking Bernoulli- and Euler-number coefficient identities, is the stated route to the two general log-sine theorem families.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Iterated integration of the arcsine series produces log-sine moment identities
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Starting from the central-binomial expansion of arcsin(x)/x, the source integrates and differentiates to obtain related series, then constructs a polylogarithm-like hierarchy K_m(x). Repeated integration by parts and the substitution x=sin(theta/2) turn the hierarchy into integrals of powers of log(2x), hence log-sine moments.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Imaginary substitution creates the inverse-hyperbolic-sine companion hierarchy
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Replacing x by ix in the arcsine identities produces inverse-hyperbolic-sine series. The source builds an analogous F_m hierarchy and, after integration by parts, connects the resulting central-binomial sums to log-sinh moments. This explains structurally why the circular and hyperbolic integral families occur in parallel.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Finite and infinite horizon produce different proved scaling laws in two dimensions
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The source distinguishes established results: bounded free paths yield Brownian scaling proportional to t, whereas infinite corridors retain Gaussian limits with the nonstandard t log t scale. It also separates discrete-time proofs from continuous-time convergence and fixes the order of the small-scatterer and long-time limits used later.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Macroscopic diffusivity, microscopic moments, and Gaussian covariance
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The diffusion PDE, its Gaussian Green function, and the displacement second moment establish the conventional relation between diffusivity matrix D and limiting covariance Sigma=2D. The unit fixes factors and distinguishes moment convergence from weak convergence.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Weak convergence need not determine anomalous second moments
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: For logarithmic superdiffusion the source defines a moment coefficient D and a limiting-law covariance Xi separately, then explains why slowly spreading tails can make weak convergence compatible with nonconvergent or differently normalized moments. It also contrasts continuous-time slow correlations with discrete-time infinite single-flight variance.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Finite-time Gaussian cores coexist with ballistic expanding tails
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Figure 1 numerically shows convergence of the scaled core toward a normal law while lattice oscillations and collision-free ballistic spikes remain in expanding tails. This is source evidence for the mechanism by which moments can exceed the covariance seen in the weak limit.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Rare free flights predict a factor-two separation between moment and limit-law coefficients
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Exact corridor formulas from the literature are reconciled by a heuristic tail cutoff: collision-free probability decays only like 1/t, so the converged Gaussian core captures half of the logarithmic second moment. The author therefore proposes Xi=D rather than the normal-diffusion relation Xi=2D.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Horizon dimension and collision-free survival organize long flights
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The source replaces a binary finite/infinite classification with sets of collision-free phase points carrying a velocity subspace dimension. It defines horizon-specific survival FH(t) and distinguishes maximal, principal, and incipient horizons, predicting which dimensions can contribute to leading survival and superdiffusion.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Conjecture 1: non-incipient maximal horizons dominate survival
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The conjecture asserts that the leading free-flight probability is the finite sum of maximal non-incipient horizon contributions, treating incipient horizons, lower-dimensional horizons, and overlaps as subleading. The source explicitly identifies this as a geometric, not dynamical, unproved step.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Conditional survival asymptotic as a sum of visibility integrals
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Theorem 1 combines Conjecture 1 with two later lemmas to express the leading free-flight probability through horizon dimension, lattice covolume, and a visibility-counting double integral. It converts global survival into finite local geometric contributions.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Conjecture 2: incipient horizons create a critical dimension at six
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Heuristic summation and later simulations motivate t^-2 decay below dimension six, an additional logarithm at six, and an unknown fractional exponent between one and two above six.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Conjecture 3: colliding trajectories decorrelate below the free-flight scale
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: A grazing-collision scaling argument motivates that correlations from trajectories with at least one collision are little-o of the collision-free survival probability. This isolates uninterrupted flights as the leading correlation mechanism needed for diffusion.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Principal horizons determine the superdiffusion matrix and link it to survival
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Conditional on Conjectures 1 and 3, Theorem 2 sums projected horizon directions weighted by squared widths to obtain D. Taking the trace and combining with Theorem 1 yields the geometry-independent relation dD=lim tF(t), while incomplete spanning predicts degenerate superdiffusion.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: The initial RH connection is explicitly formal rather than an equivalence proof
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The author explains that small scatterers generate increasing lattice-horizon sums whose Mellin transforms contain inverse zeta factors. The proposed RH link requires contour closure along pole-avoiding semicircles, and the source explicitly says that a complete equivalence proof is unavailable even for a simpler analogue.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Phase space, collision time, and survival sets
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The compact quotient phase space, invariant probability measure, billiard flow, next-collision time, and survivor set Mt make the free-flight function F(t) an exact measure-theoretic object. Zero-measure collision ambiguities are separated from the asymptotic problem.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Horizons arise from rational velocity subspaces and connected spatial components
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Free torus trajectories either become dense or lie parallel to lattice-spanned subspaces. The source uses this dichotomy to construct velocity sets, quotient the spatial direction, and define an inextensible horizon with connected spatial projection; examples show why one direction can support multiple horizons.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Incipient horizons contain infinitely many lower-dimensional horizon directions
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Maximal and principal horizons are dimension-based, while an incipient horizon has zero transverse measure. In dimensions above two, shrinking a higher-dimensional horizon creates a lattice of tangencies and countably many subordinate horizon directions, explaining why naive finite dominance fails at the transition.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Only finitely many maximal horizons exist
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Lemma 1 proves finiteness by showing that infinitely many connected components conflict with finitely many convex scatterer pieces, while infinitely many increasingly dense velocity subspaces force a larger horizon and contradict maximality.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: A two-dimensional corridor covering proposition fails in higher dimensions
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Long paths in higher dimensions can traverse a complicated connected network of horizons of different dimensions, so Bleher's bounded-exception corridor proposition cannot be reused. Intersections, non-maximal horizons, and infinitely many subhorizons in the incipient case are exactly the omissions delegated to Conjecture 1.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: A single horizon contributes a visibility-weighted power law
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Lemma 2 decomposes position and velocity into parallel and perpendicular components, rescales transverse velocities by 1/t, and integrates the visible transverse region to prove FH(t) decays as t^{-(d-dH)} with an explicit geometric coefficient.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Primitive dual vectors enumerate principal horizons with a width cutoff
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Codimension-one horizon lattices correspond to primitive dual-lattice vectors modulo sign. For spherical scatterers the horizon exists exactly below a length cutoff and has width L^-1-2r; inserting these widths into conditional Theorem 1 yields the explicit finite lattice sum for F(t).

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Dimension-wide simulations test the horizon-sum survival laws
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The source describes collision computation, boundary-accuracy safeguards, and precision checks, then compares dimensions 2-10. Results support C/t for principal horizons and qualitatively support C/t^2 for overlapping-scatterer lower-dimensional horizons, with explicitly worsening statistics and convergence at high dimension.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Mobius inversion and Mellin transform expose inverse-zeta poles
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Mobius inversion removes the primitive-vector constraint, and a Mellin transform converts the cutoff lattice sum into a contour integral containing an Epstein zeta numerator and 1/zeta(s+1). Residue expansion would translate poles into small-r powers.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: RH controls the proposed small-scatterer remainder, conditional on contour closure
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Known analytic properties of Epstein zeta locate the numerator's pole and zeros, while zeros of zeta(s+1) create denominator poles. Under the unproved contour step, the leading Boltzmann-Grad term has an O(r^{1/2-delta}) remainder for every positive delta if RH holds; numerical residue sums support the smooth real-pole terms, and the source only suggests an equivalence.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Rational multi-scatterer cells introduce Dirichlet characters and a GRH analogy
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: For rationally located multiple scatterers, the Mellin calculation is said to replace the scalar sums by Dirichlet L-functions and twisted Epstein zeta functions, creating a formal route from transport to generalized RH.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Incipient-horizon rescaling produces an L^-5 contribution and critical summability threshold
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: At touching radius, each incipient coordinate plane contains horizons indexed by all primitive lattice vectors. Rescaling the two-dimensional transverse gap yields a universal four-parabola region; its visibility integral is numerically estimated and gives FH(t) proportional to t^-2 L^-5. Summing indices becomes an Epstein series convergent through dimension five and divergent from six.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Fitted survival exponents support a change near dimension six
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Figure 7 and Table 2 compare dimensions 2-10 at touching radius. Low dimensions approach exponent two, while dimensions six and above show smaller fitted exponents, qualitatively supporting Conjecture 2 while revealing strong finite-time drift.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Velocity correlations are compared directly with free-flight predictions
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The source tests Conjecture 3 by fitting velocity autocorrelation to C_r/t and comparing C_r with the horizon-sum limit of tF(t) across scatterer radii. This is the empirical bridge from collision-free geometry to diffusion.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Proof of Theorem 2 reduces correlations to constant-velocity horizon integrals
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Assuming Conjecture 3 removes colliding trajectories at leading order and Conjecture 1 replaces survivors by maximal horizons. Repeating the transverse scaling of Lemma 2 and integrating vv over the horizon sphere gives the projection matrix and completes Theorem 2.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Explicit cubic diffusivity inherits the same formal RH remainder
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: For ranges with specified horizon families the conditional theorem yields explicit isotropic diffusivity. In the fixed-d, small-r limit the survival relation transfers equation (31)'s RH-sensitive remainder directly to D.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Mean free time transfers continuous covariance to collision-time covariance
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The source distinguishes the formally infinite discrete moment coefficient from the finite covariance of the limiting law, uses the mean free time to relate discrete and continuous covariance, and derives a simplified horizon sum for the discrete-time covariance.

section_argument_map.label: Title and abstract
section_argument_map.mathematical_role: Announces multidimensional infinite-horizon diffusion, conditional formulas, numerical simulations, a proposed critical dimension, and an RH connection.

section_argument_map.label: 1. Introduction
section_argument_map.mathematical_role: Reviews proved two-dimensional finite/infinite-horizon limit laws and defines the higher-dimensional scope and order of limits.

section_argument_map.label: 2. Diffusion coefficients
section_argument_map.mathematical_role: Separates moment-defined diffusivity from limiting-law covariance in logarithmic superdiffusion and proposes a rare-flight explanation for their discrepancy.

section_argument_map.label: Figure 2 and 3. Summary of results
section_argument_map.mathematical_role: Introduces horizon taxonomy, states three conjectures and two conditional theorems, and explicitly qualifies the formal RH connection.

section_argument_map.label: 4. Definitions
section_argument_map.mathematical_role: Defines phase space, free-flight survival, horizons, maximal/principal/incipient status, and the infinite lower-dimensional structure attached to incipient horizons.

section_argument_map.label: 5. Two lemmas
section_argument_map.mathematical_role: Proves finiteness of maximal horizons, explains why a two-dimensional proposition fails to generalize, and proves each non-incipient horizon's survival asymptotic.

section_argument_map.label: 6. Principal horizons and the free flight function
section_argument_map.mathematical_role: Enumerates horizons by primitive dual-lattice vectors, derives the survival lattice sum, tests it numerically, and uses Mellin inversion to formulate a conditional RH/GRH-sensitive small-scatterer expansion.

section_argument_map.label: 7. Incipient horizons and the critical dimension
section_argument_map.mathematical_role: Derives a limiting cusp geometry and horizon-sum convergence threshold, then uses simulations to support a conjectured change of decay at dimension six.

section_argument_map.label: 8. Correlations and diffusion
section_argument_map.mathematical_role: Tests the decorrelation conjecture numerically, proves the conditional superdiffusion theorem, and transfers the formal RH remainder to diffusivity.

section_argument_map.label: 9. Diffusion in discrete time
section_argument_map.mathematical_role: Relates continuous-time covariance to collision-time covariance through the mean free time and gives the resulting horizon formula.

section_argument_map.label: Acknowledgements and references
section_argument_map.mathematical_role: Non-mathematical acknowledgements and bibliography.

notation_and_main_objects_policy: Notation is intentionally not reconstructed mechanically; use the exact unit and nearby source context. Unit titles/types provide routing hints only.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: A symmetry-preserving polynomial transform creates a critical-line zero problem
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The linear transform maps monomials to rising-factorial polynomials and has an integral representation; symmetric input gives the functional equation T[g](s)=T[g](1−s). The source defines a polynomial ‘Riemann hypothesis’ as all zeros lying on Re(s)=1/2 and cites a prior preservation theorem when the input already has that property.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: The quadratic transform leads to a four-term recurrence and an unproved interlacing RH analogue
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: For powers of x(x−1)+r, the transformed polynomial becomes a real polynomial in u=−t² on the critical line. Numerical evidence suggests negative real zeros and interlacing, but the four-term recurrence lacks standard orthogonality. An asymptotic renormalization compresses n,r dependence to one parameter C and motivates a threshold conjecture.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: One critical Hankel sequence links recurrences, integrals, determinants, ASMs, and two path models
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The introduction isolates the sequence 1,3,26,646,45885 and states the later proved identities Δ=I=A=RR, V=O, and A=P. It also identifies a still-missing direct bijection between the osculating and non-intersecting path families as an alternative combinatorial proof of the vertically symmetric ASM formula.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Renormalization replaces the original n-dependent recurrence by q_n=xq_{n−1}−Cq_{n−2}−q_{n−3}
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The section records the exact original four-term recurrence and the normalized one-parameter recurrence obtained by the appendix transformations, with the original r range mapped toward a critical limiting value C=3.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Three-term positivity forces interlacing, but four-term functionals lose the needed orthogonality
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The standard three-term recurrence yields a positive-definite orthogonality functional exactly when its recurrence coefficients are positive, hence simple real interlacing zeros and positive Hankel determinants. The analogous functional for the four-term recurrence annihilates each q_n but not cross-products, identifying why the classical proof cannot transfer.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: The 3-Conjecture asserts an iff threshold, while Theorem 1 proves only C≥3
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Conjecture 1 claims real zeros exactly for C≥3 and interlacing in that regime. The source proves sufficiency but reports only numerical non-real zeros below 3, including near C=2.9, leaving necessity open.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: A continuity transition and characteristic-root case split prove interlacing for C≥3
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: For fixed finite N, large C gives a perturbation of orthogonal polynomials. Any first loss of strict interlacing must create a common real root of consecutive q’s. Solving the recurrence at that root through a cubic characteristic equation forces a repeated characteristic root; distinct, double, and triple-root cases show such a transition cannot occur at or above 3.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: The 6-Conjecture proposes a C≥6 threshold for a five-term recurrence
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: A representative higher-order recurrence is conjectured to have real interlacing zeros exactly above the binomial-looking threshold 6, suggesting a wider family of critical coefficients.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: One recurrence functional has nine algebraic, combinatorial, and analytic moment forms
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Theorem 2 identifies the moments of the four-term functional as an inverse coefficient-matrix entry, weighted excursions, 2–3 trees, a Lagrange coefficient, an explicit sum, a positive real integral for C≥3, and three special C=3 integral/binomial expressions. This is the principal bridge from recurrence theory to combinatorics.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Inverse coefficients become weighted paths, 2–3 trees, and a Lagrange functional equation
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The proof inverts the recurrence coefficient matrix, reads its recursion as a weighted nonnegative path model, bijects paths with depth-first codes of 2–3 trees, and decomposes trees into two or three principal subtrees. Lagrange inversion then supplies the coefficient and multinomial moment formulas; a contour-generating-function derivation gives an independent check.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Contour deformation yields a positive real moment density exactly in the C≥3 regime
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The contour representation is analyzed through the cubic inverse map and its discriminant. For C>3, branch points and cycles permit deformation to a real interval where the branch jump defines a positive density; the degenerate C=3 case follows by a limit and explicit substitutions.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Further substitutions convert critical moments to fractional-binomial sums and degree data
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The proof transforms the C=3 integral to a beta-type integral, producing the remaining fractional-binomial expression; the final form is stated with details omitted. Path and multinomial views then determine degrees and leading Catalan/binomial coefficients of the moment polynomials.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Critical Hankel data match vertically symmetric ASM counts and suggest a positive t-statistic
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: At C=3 the moment Hankel determinants compute the striking ASM-number prefix. Explicit low-n polynomials Δ_n(3+t) have nonnegative coefficients even though Δ_n(C) does not; the authors conjecturally interpret t as a statistic on a larger object class.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: A positive functional can support a four-term recurrence with non-real zeros
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Starting from Hermite orthogonality, the authors perturb finitely many basis polynomials so the same positive functional annihilates the new recurrence sequence, then choose explicit parameters making q_4 vanish at a non-real point. This disproves the naive extension of the three-term positivity criterion.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Andreief/Vandermonde symmetrization turns Δ_n into a Macdonald-type integral
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Substituting the one-variable moment integral into the Hankel determinant and symmetrizing over variables converts the product of two determinants to a squared Vandermonde, yielding Theorem 3’s multiple integral I_n.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Termwise beta evaluation gives a binomial-moment determinant
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Expanding the squared Vandermonde and evaluating each density moment by beta/gamma identities identifies Δ_n with a Hankel determinant whose entries are explicit integer binomial expressions, illustrated through n=2.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Row operations produce four equivalent Hankel moment sequences, one parameter-independent
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Theorem 4 transforms the original moments to explicit binomial sequences and a polynomial family b_k(x). A Carlitz recurrence plus degree counting shows det[b_{i+j}(x)] is independent of x, so specializations yield three further Hankel forms.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Equivalent t-deformed Hankel entries are proposed but not constructed
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The observed nonnegative Δ_n(3+t) coefficients motivate the idea that each equivalent critical moment sequence should admit a polynomial t-deformation with the same determinant.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: An LDU ansatz and WZ certificates evaluate Δ_n as the Robbins–Rumsey product
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Theorem 5 chooses an explicit lower-triangular multiplier that should triangularize the binomial Hankel matrix, reducing the determinant to diagonal factors matching RR(n). The required off-diagonal and diagonal multisums are certified by Wilf–Zeilberger-style recurrences generated with automated tools.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Vertically symmetric ASMs realize the Robbins–Rumsey sequence by an external theorem
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The section defines ASMs, recalls the general enumeration, and states the product for odd-size vertically symmetric ASMs. The product is the same RR(n) evaluated by Theorem 5.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Sign-reversing involutions count non-intersecting paths, while corner sums encode ASMs as osculating paths
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The source reviews the Lindström-style signed path determinant and its path-tail switching involution, then converts ASM row/column partial-sum constraints into level boundaries of the corner-sum matrix. Those boundaries form osculating rather than non-intersecting paths.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Vertically symmetric ASMs are bijective with a fixed osculating-path ensemble
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Lemma 2 restricts the corner-sum construction to half of a vertically symmetric ASM, where the central column and boundary data force specified starts and ends. The remaining cell boundaries give an osculating family, and the map is reversible.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: A two-stage cancellation rescues a path determinant when the standard endpoint criterion fails
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Theorem 6 interprets a family of binomial Hankel determinants. Because non-identity path matchings can be non-intersecting, ordinary tail-switching is insufficient; a first involution uses a binomial divisibility bijection to cancel paths beginning with too many vertical steps, after which standard intersection cancellation leaves exactly ordered non-intersecting paths.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Hankel paths realize the ASM-number determinant and yield a Catalan determinant proof
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The r=2 specialization defines P_n and proves it equals the critical binomial determinant. A related two-stage symmetric involution shows another central-binomial Hankel determinant counts 2^n right-angle path families, while the r=1 case gives a combinatorial proof that a Catalan Hankel determinant equals one.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Both path models admit tableau encodings, but their equality lacks a direct bijection
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Non-intersecting Hankel paths correspond to bounded column-strict staircase tableaux, while osculating ASM paths correspond to strict Gelfand patterns or shifted ‘good’ tableaux. These parallel encodings sharpen the proposed bijection problem.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: C=6 determinants have alternate binomial forms, while broader smoothness patterns appear to fail
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The five-term critical recurrence defines a moment functional whose first Hankel determinants match a higher-r binomial determinant row. Numerical factorization suggests the exceptional smooth product behavior at low orders does not persist for general binomial parameters a≥4.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: A multidimensional twisted transform preserves polynomial critical-line zeros, but interlacing remains open
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: The epilogue generalizes the one-variable transform to a coupled multidimensional kernel and cites a proof that critical-line-rooted input polynomials yield a critical-line-rooted output. The expected interlacing phenomenon and associated combinatorics are deferred.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Differentiating a transformed integral derives the original four-term recurrence
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Appendix I embeds the transform in a one-parameter group of interval maps, differentiates its multiplier at the identity, and specializes to powers of a quadratic. Differential identities for those powers produce the exact n,r-dependent four-term recurrence and indicate a route to higher-order recurrences.

result_and_mechanism_map.title: Successive asymptotic scalings explain—but do not rigorously transfer—the critical C=3 model
result_and_mechanism_map.why_material: Appendix II sets s=1/2+it and u=−t², then divides by n², discards vanishing coefficient terms, rescales variables and polynomials, and replaces n-dependent arguments to obtain a constant-coefficient four-term recurrence. The r>1/4 range maps to C>3, explaining why 3 emerged as the normalized threshold.

source_identity.title: From a Polynomial Riemann Hypothesis to Alternating Sign Matrices

within_source_synthesis_map.claim: For the normalized four-term recurrence, C=3 is simultaneously the proved onset of real interlacing, the degenerate endpoint of a positive integral density, and the parameter where the Hankel determinants acquire the vertically symmetric ASM sequence.
within_source_synthesis_map.limit: Only the normalized recurrence theorem and moment/determinant facts are proved; the passage back to the original quadratic polynomial RH is heuristic, and the general t-statistic interpretation is conjectural.
within_source_synthesis_map.title: The critical value C=3 sits at three different interfaces

within_source_synthesis_map.claim: Three-term recurrences use positive orthogonality to force interlacing, whereas the four-term functional loses cross-orthogonality; the special C≥3 sequence still interlaces by a transition argument, but an explicit Hermite-based construction shows positivity alone cannot explain it.
within_source_synthesis_map.limit: The counterexample rules out a general positivity criterion, not a more specialized higher-order structure for this recurrence.
within_source_synthesis_map.title: Positivity and real-rootedness decouple beyond three-term orthogonality

within_source_synthesis_map.claim: The same moments arise from inverse recurrence coefficients, weighted excursions, 2–3 trees, Lagrange inversion, contour jumps, positive densities, beta integrals, and explicit binomial sequences; taking their Hankel determinant transports identities between these domains.
within_source_synthesis_map.limit: Some late fractional-binomial details are omitted locally, and exact analytic branch manipulations are formula-dependent.
within_source_synthesis_map.title: A recurrence moment is a hub of representations

within_source_synthesis_map.claim: Critical Hankel determinants equal the Robbins–Rumsey product by a computer-assisted triangularization, prior work equates that product with vertically symmetric ASMs, and this paper separately models the two sides by non-intersecting and osculating paths. A direct bijection between those path/tableau families would replace the product-mediated equality.
within_source_synthesis_map.limit: No direct bijection is given, and the diagonal WZ certificate needed to audit the determinant evaluation is external to the source.
within_source_synthesis_map.title: The ASM equality chain is proved algebraically but lacks the desired direct bijection

within_source_synthesis_map.claim: When ordinary path-tail switching leaves non-identity non-intersecting matchings, a preliminary sign-reversing involution removes a structurally forbidden boundary or symmetry class; standard intersection cancellation then exposes a positive fixed-point family counted by the determinant.
within_source_synthesis_map.limit: The first involution in Theorem 6 depends on choosing a combinatorial division bijection that is not made explicit, limiting direct constructivity.
within_source_synthesis_map.title: Nonstandard endpoint geometry calls for layered involutions

within_source_synthesis_map.claim: Functional equations about s↔1−s motivate asking whether polynomial zeros lie on Re(s)=1/2; variable changes turn this into real-root/interlacing problems for recurrence polynomials, with threshold conjectures and one proved normalized case.
within_source_synthesis_map.limit: None of these results bears directly on the truth of the Riemann hypothesis for ζ, and several advertised analogues remain numerical or conjectural.
within_source_synthesis_map.title: Polynomial RH terminology names a finite zero analogy, not zeta evidence
